summary:
Giresun province stands under the national framework of Türkiye. The source inventory contains no Giresun-specific finding on trans rights, so every assessment below describes national law and practice that applies inside the province.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise LGBT conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with up to 3 years' imprisonment, and would criminalise same-sex ceremonies with up to 4 years. The same package would raise the eligibility age for gender-affirming healthcare from 18 to 25, add mandatory infertility and repeated-evaluation conditions, and expose providers to fines and up to 7 years' imprisonment and patients to up to 3 years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected to the draft. It had not been enacted when reported, but authorities have acted as though its prohibitions were already in force.

The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, including 299 detention decisions: 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record. The Erdoğan government has repeatedly framed its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people.

Street-level enforcement falls directly on documents. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue those checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police took no fine but documented her anyway, and that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already applied to her. Turkey also requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Any checkpoint interaction is therefore an occasion on which a visitor's documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Türkiye is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Police have banned Pride marches in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

The document and status baseline is longer established: homosexuality has been decriminalised since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, the same year gender-reassignment surgery became legal.

Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, while accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025. The Prison Insider country profile on Türkiye, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners; there is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, risking profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.
tangentialFactors:
The direction of travel is documented and adverse. A leaked draft that would effectively criminalise LGBT conduct was before the government as of October 2025, yet enforcement described above preceded any enactment, which separates the practical risk in Giresun from the status of the statute book.

Historical depth is established rather than recent. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people; it predates legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.

Comparative standing is weak by regional measures. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking placed Turkey 47th out of 49 countries.

The framework is uneven in a way that matters for expectations: decriminalisation dates to 1858 and legal gender recognition to 1988, yet there is no comprehensive national law banning discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, LGBTQ people are barred from openly serving in the military, and same-sex marriage, civil unions and joint adoption are not recognised.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change and gender-reassignment surgery have been available in Türkiye since 1988, so residents can obtain matched documents; the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation and the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that preceded it constrain how transition care is recorded and reported.

A court case to close the association Lambda Istanbul was overruled by the Constitutional Court, keeping the organisation open.

Residents who join Pride events face bans in most years since 2015 in Istanbul and other cities, with tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions used against participants; the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week monitoring found that violations recorded since 2015 continued.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement, with transfers disrupting visits and solidarity networks and complaints able to attract further violence. The death of the transgender prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025 drew demands for an independent investigation from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın, and the case was raised in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Detention of LGBT people is recorded at scale: 313 violations and 299 detention decisions in 2025, including 43 taken off the record.
outOfScopeNotes:
No usable finding for Giresun itself was recorded in the source inventory, so province-level policing, facilities and local practice in Giresun remain not sourced; the assessment rests on the national framework that applies there.

The 11th Judicial Package was a leaked draft as of the 29 October 2025 reporting and had not been enacted at that point; whether it has since been passed is unresolved here.

The current reach of the Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, and whether it restricts care in Giresun, is not sourced.
